title: The paper-clip transistor
hook: The first transistor was germanium, gold foil and a spring bent from a paper clip.
peek: In December 1947, two scientists at Bell Labs made a crude device that could amplify an electrical signal. It was built from a chip of germanium, a strip of gold foil and a bent paper clip, and it was the first transistor.
lede: In December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working at Bell Labs in New Jersey, built a device that would change electronics. Brattain wrapped gold foil around a small plastic triangle, slit it at the tip with a razor blade and pressed it onto a slab of germanium using a spring made from a paper clip. The point-contact transistor worked.

bullets.text: On 23 December 1947 Bardeen and Brattain showed it to Bell Labs managers. Speaking into a microphone, they used the transistor to make a voice louder in a pair of headphones.

Their group leader, William Shockley, was frustrated not to have been part of the breakthrough. Within weeks he worked out the junction transistor, a sturdier design that soon replaced the point-contact version.
Bell Labs held an internal vote on a name. The winner, transistor, was suggested by the engineer John Pierce. He based it on transresistance, though it is often explained as transfer plus resistor.
Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956. Bardeen later won a second physics prize, for superconductivity, the only person to do so.
